conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes that the claim is supported by evidence, citing a randomized controlled trial (ACTIVE trial) showing an 86% relative risk reduction in new vertebral fractures over 18 months, as well as FDA labeling and clinical practice guidelines.
conclusion.label: endorses

report:
## Conclusion

The claim is **supported, not false**—with an important scope: evidence concerns **new radiographically detected (morphometric) vertebral fractures over 18 months** in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, rather than proving benefit for every type of symptomatic fracture or every patient population.

The key evidence is the phase 3, randomized, placebo-controlled ACTIVE trial. Its published conclusion was that subcutaneous abaloparatide reduced new vertebral and nonvertebral fractures versus placebo over 18 months. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27533157/

The FDA-approved label reports the vertebral-fracture result quantitatively: **0.6%** of abaloparatide-treated women versus **4.2%** of placebo-treated women had a new vertebral fracture at 18 months (**p < 0.0001**). That is an absolute reduction of about **3.6 percentage points** and a relative reduction of about **86%**. https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2017/208743lbl.pdf

Independent clinical guidance is consistent with this evidence: the Endocrine Society recommends teriparatide or abaloparatide for up to two years in postmenopausal women at *very high* fracture risk to reduce vertebral and nonvertebral fractures. https://www.endocrine.org/clinical-practice-guidelines/osteoporosis-in-postmenopausal-women

Thus, a reasonable critique would be that the magnitude and applicability depend on the studied high-risk population, 18-month duration, and morphometric endpoint—not that abaloparatide lacks evidence of vertebral-fracture reduction.
